title: Robustness: The Cash Result Without the Dynamic Term
section_job: The cash-ratio regressions carry the cash ratio's own one-quarter lag (partial adjustment) with firm fixed effects. A dynamic panel of this kind is subject to the Nickell bias, which the within transformation induces and which is not confined to the lag coefficient alone (it also contaminates regressors correlated with lagged cash, including the event-time bins). The guard is not to reason about the size of the bias but to remove the dynamic term: re-estimate the cash column with static fixed effects (a level estimand). The timing pattern is preserved (no fall at announcement, the pre-announcement-to-gap change is 0.0012 below zero and insignificant, like the with-lag 0.0006; a fall at completion, gap-to-completion 0.0318, significant at one percent; pre-announcement-to-completion decline 0.0305 against the with-lag 0.0216). Magnitudes are larger because the specification shifts from a change to a level interpretation, so only the qualitative timing carries over. The lag stays in the main specification. The static specification carries no lagged dependent variable and hence no dynamic-panel bias, so the timing conclusion holds with or without the term that carries it; removing the lag sidesteps the bias rather than fixing it.
spine: P1 the design property: the cash regressions are a dynamic fixed-effects panel, subject to the Nickell bias, which is not confined to the lag coefficient, so the guard is to remove the dynamic term (the residual carries no lag and is the anchor). P2 the test: drop the lag, re-estimate with static fixed effects, a level estimand, so read the timing pattern not the magnitude. P3 result: timing preserved (no fall at announcement, 0.0012 below zero and insignificant; fall at completion 0.0318; pre-announcement-to-completion 0.0305), magnitudes larger because level not change; residual unchanged. P4 reading: the lag stays in the main specification (cash is sticky); the static specification has no lag and hence no dynamic-panel bias, so the timing conclusion holds with or without the dynamic term.
register_global: correlational, no causal identification; two-tailed throughout.
Author voice. No mention of a reader, a referee, an audit, or a hypothetical critic, in any prose or the title. The work has not been refereed.
Do not quantify or call the Nickell bias small or negligible (the large-T trap). Name it as a standard concept (an eponym), with no citation, matching how Section 2.4 treats clustering methods.

The Nickell bias is not confined to the lag coefficient: the within transformation contaminates correlated regressors, including the bins, since cash trends up before the deal. Do not argue that not interpreting the lag immunizes the bins. The real guard is removing the dynamic term (advisor, 2026-06-15).

Dropping the lag sidesteps the bias (the static specification has no lagged dependent variable, hence no dynamic-panel bias); it does not fix the bias. The honest claim is that the timing conclusion holds with or without the dynamic term.

Magnitudes are not robust; they are about forty percent larger without the lag because the estimand shifts from a change (partial adjustment) to a level. Only the timing pattern carries over. Never write robust to dropping the lag.

The cash level specification has the gap coefficient (0.0128) above the pre-announcement one (0.0116), so the pre-announcement quarter is not the cash peak. Name cash contrasts plainly (pre-announcement-to-gap, gap-to-completion, pre-announcement-to-completion). Reserve the word peak for the residual.
The lag stays in the main specification: cash is sticky, and partial adjustment is the right model.

paragraphs.final_prose: The cash-ratio regressions of Sections~3.3 and~3.4 include the cash ratio's own one-quarter lag alongside firm fixed effects, a partial-adjustment form that suits a sticky stock like cash. A dynamic panel of this kind, a lagged dependent variable estimated with fixed effects, is subject to the Nickell bias, which the within transformation induces and which is not confined to the coefficient on the lag alone. Rather than reason about the size of that bias, we guard against it directly, by removing the dynamic term and re-estimating without it. The residual outcome carries no lag and is unaffected, so it serves here as an anchor.

intent.statement: State the test and what carries over. Re-estimate the cash column with static fixed effects, dropping the lagged dependent variable (point to the table). Removing the lag changes what the coefficients describe: with the lag each coefficient is a change in the cash ratio around its own recent level (a partial adjustment); without it the coefficients describe the level of the cash ratio relative to the baseline. The two specifications are on different scales, so the comparison that carries over is the timing pattern, the sign and significance of the bins across event time, not the size of any single coefficient.

paragraphs.final_prose: We re-estimate the cash column with static fixed effects, dropping the lagged dependent variable; Table~\ref{tab:empire_drop_staticfe} reports it. Removing the lag changes what the cash coefficients describe. With the lag, each coefficient is a change in the cash ratio around its own recent level, a partial adjustment; without it, the coefficients describe the level of the cash ratio relative to the baseline. The two specifications are therefore on different scales, and the comparison that carries over is the timing pattern, the sign and significance of the bins across event time, not the size of any single coefficient.

intent.statement: Report the result. The pre-announcement-to-completion decline is 0.0305 (p<.01), larger than the 0.0216 of the partial-adjustment specification, as expected when the coefficients describe a level rather than a change. The residual column is unchanged, since it never carried the lag.

paragraphs.final_prose: The timing pattern is the same. Without the lag the cash ratio does not fall when the deal is announced, the pre-announcement-to-gap change of $-0.0012$ being insignificant just as the partial-adjustment change of $0.0006$ was, and it falls only once the cash leaves at completion, by $0.0318$ from the gap to completion ($p<0.01$), with a completion coefficient of $-0.0189$ ($p<0.01$). The pre-announcement-to-completion decline is $0.0305$ ($p<0.01$), larger than the $0.0216$ of the partial-adjustment specification, as expected when the coefficients describe a level rather than a change. The residual column is unchanged, as it must be, since it never carried the lag.

intent.statement: State the reading. The lag belongs in the main specification, because cash is sticky and partial adjustment is the right description of how it moves; the static specification is not a better model but a check that removes the dynamic term entirely. Because the static specification carries no lagged dependent variable, it carries no dynamic-panel bias, so the cash timing conclusion, no fall at announcement and a fall at completion, holds whether or not that term is present. The timing of the cash path, on which the differential-timing result rests, does not ride on the dynamic specification.
